title: The Novelty Mirage: When LLM Judges Grade LLM Hypotheses

body:
In August 2024 Sakana AI published *The AI Scientist*, a pipeline that reads a problem statement, produces an idea, writes the code that tests it, then drafts and reviews the paper it just wrote. The demo made two claims that sat uneasily together. Its automated reviewer hit balanced accuracy of $69%$ on ICLR-style ratings, close to inter-human agreement in the NeurIPS 2021 consistency study. And several of the ideas the system rated as novel were not novel at all — one flagged idea was *micro-batching for SGD*, an optimizer trick that has been in every deep-learning textbook since 2015. Reviewer calibrated on paper reviews, ideation confidently wrong on ideas. *How can the same class of system be reliable in one role and delusional in the other?* That is the question this post is about.

The pattern generalizes past Sakana. Every LLM-based scientific-discovery pipeline now shipping — Google DeepMind's Co-Scientist (*Nature*, 2026), BioDisco (Ke et al., 2025), BioVerge (2025) — has a *self-scoring* loop somewhere in it. Candidates are drafted by a model and ranked by a model, sometimes the same model. That inner loop is the part users interact with least and rely on most. Recent work suggests it is also the part that is quietly rigged.

## Why the pipeline breaks quietly

Which hypothesis becomes an experiment is what these systems are for. A wet-lab bench costs money, a compute run costs GPU-hours, a graduate student's year costs a graduate student's year — so the top-of-list judgment is the point at which errors turn into human time. If that judgment is systematically biased toward outputs sharing the generator's stylistic and lexical distribution — and away from human-written baselines that read differently — the system is not accelerating discovery. It is redirecting attention toward a subspace of ideas that *look like an LLM wrote them*.

The phenomenon has a name now. Zhu et al.'s *On the Limits of LLM-as-Judge for Scientific Novelty Assessment* (arXiv 2606.12071, June 2026) call it the **novelty mirage**: LLM judges consistently rate model-generated research questions as highly novel, and the preference *strengthens* under comparative (pairwise) judging even though pairwise setups are usually supposed to be more calibrated. Domain experts, given the same pairs, invert the ranking: they prefer the author-anchored reference questions, describing the model-generated ones as narrow, source-bound, or a paraphrase of the paper's own contribution restated as a question. Two graders, same rubric, opposite orderings. Not a noise problem; a construct-validity problem.

## What novelty is, formally, and where the judge slips

Fix a hypothesis $h$ written in natural language, and a background corpus of prior work $\mathcal{C} = {c_1, \ldots, c_M}$. Any operationalization of *novelty* must be a functional of $h$ and $\mathcal{C}$. Three standard families:

**Retrieval-based novelty.** Let $\phi$ be a sentence encoder and define

$$s_{\text{ret}}(h; \mathcal{C}) = 1 - \max_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \cos!\big(\phi(h), \phi(c)\big).$$

A hypothesis is novel to the extent it is *far* from its nearest neighbour in prior work. This is what most Literature-Based Discovery (LBD) systems and RAG-style ideation pipelines report, sometimes with a top-$k$ average instead of the max.

**Concept-graph novelty.** Extract entity or relation tuples from $h$ and from every $c$, then measure novelty as the fraction of *edges* — pairs $(e_i, e_j)$ or triplets $(e_i, r, e_j)$ — in $h$'s tuple set that do not co-occur in any $c$. This is the Swansonian LBD form, and BioVerge (Sun et al., 2025, arXiv 2511.08866) still runs on a variant of it using PubTator3 triples.

**LLM-as-judge novelty.** Prompt an LLM with $h$ and either (a) a Likert rubric (1–5 novelty), (b) a reference $h^\star$ and ask for a comparative preference, or (c) $h$ and a small retrieved neighbourhood ${c_{i_1}, \ldots, c_{i_k}}$ and ask for a scored critique. This is what almost every co-scientist pipeline uses internally and what almost every meta-benchmark uses externally.

The mirage lives in the third family. Two mechanisms are load-bearing.

*The lexical–stylistic collision.* Let $q_G$ be the generator's next-token distribution and $q_J$ the judge's. In every deployed pipeline these are similar — same model, same base with a fine-tune, or two frontier models trained on massively overlapping corpora. The judge's novelty score $\hat{s}_J(h)$ is, under any reasonable prompt, monotone in the judge's fluency-adjusted read of $h$: outputs the judge would have written itself score high on "these are the exact framings the field uses." The problem is not that model-generated $h$ are unsurprising to the judge (they are, and that should *lower* novelty). It is that they read as *well-formed research prose*, and the judge conflates readability with substance. Author-anchored baselines carry the friction of a specific paper's argumentative move, and the judge marks them down for it.

*Retrieval scope collapse.* The judge cannot verify novelty without evidence; without RAG, it hallucinates coverage. Even with retrieval scaffolding, judges assign high novelty when the retrieved neighbourhood is small, because the max in $s_{\text{ret}}$ is trivially far when there is nothing to be near. This is how the *micro-batching for SGD* miss happens: keyword-only retrieval returns a handful of recent adjacent papers, none of them the origin, and the judge concludes the concept is uncovered.

Both mechanisms compose. When $q_G \approx q_J$ and retrieval is sparse, the mirage is doubly present: the hypothesis is stylistically legible to the judge *and* the evidence set is thin enough to make the retrieval sanity check misfire.

## The evidence, laid out

The following is what the current literature actually establishes. I read abstracts and press releases in this session, not the full PDFs — arXiv was blocked from this run's egress; more on that in the further-reading note.

**RQ-Bench (Zhu et al., 2026).** Author-anchored research questions are reconstructed from cited background/gap/contribution segments of recent arXiv papers, and paired with LLM-generated questions from the same background. Under standalone Likert judging, LLM judges rate model-generated questions as more novel; under pairwise judging, the preference strengthens. Domain experts invert it.

**Truthfulness benchmarks (Xiong et al., IJCAI 2025; arXiv 2505.14599).** Most existing evaluations of LLM hypothesis generation optimize for novelty and diversity while leaving truthfulness unmeasured. The paper argues pipelines therefore drift into scientifically invalid but stylistically plausible territory — the RQ-Bench mirage from the other side. Their remedy: check whether generated hypotheses' factual constituents survive an independent literature check.

**BioDisco (Ke et al., 2025, arXiv 2508.01285).** A multi-agent system that mixes knowledge-graph and free-text retrieval and uses an internal scorer with iterative feedback, evaluated with a Bradley–Terry paired model over human raters plus a *temporal* protocol (train on literature up to $T$, evaluate on discoveries first known at $T + \Delta t$). Temporal evaluation is a genuine advance: contamination-free by construction, and the only way to distinguish "recovered what is already known" from "predicted what came next."

**BioVerge (Sun et al., 2025, arXiv 2511.08866).** A benchmark over PubTator3 triples and PubMed abstracts, with a ReAct-style agent, reporting that self-evaluation *improves* novelty and relevance. Important counter-datapoint — self-evaluation is not net-negative — but the improvement is measured against the system's own scorer, which is exactly the setup RQ-Bench argues is biased.

**ResearchBench (Liu et al., 2025, arXiv 2503.21248).** Twelve-discipline benchmark separating inspiration retrieval, hypothesis composition, and ranking. LLMs are strong at retrieval — GPT-4o places the ground-truth inspiration in the top $4%$ of candidates with probability $\approx 45.7%$ — but only moderate at composition and ranking. Diagnostic: the parts that are pattern-matching against embeddings behave well; the parts that require *judgment about what would advance the field* do not.

**Google Co-Scientist (Gottweis et al., *Nature*, 2026).** The headline successes — an in-silico prediction of a bacterial gene-transfer mechanism confirmed at Imperial College, drug-repurposing candidates for liver fibrosis validated at Stanford — are wet-lab or independent-team validations, not internal-scorer wins. That is the right thing to report, and the standard every co-scientist paper should be held to.

Composite picture: internal self-scoring flatters LLM-generated hypotheses; external evaluation is where the honest signal lives.

## A concrete anchor: what shared-prior does to novelty scores

Stripped-down model of the mirage. Generator draws $h \sim q_G$; judge scores by a proxy

$$\hat{s}*J(h) = \alpha \cdot \big(1 - \tfrac{1}{k}!\sum*{c \in \mathrm{NN}_k(h)} \cos(\phi(h), \phi(c))\big) + \beta \cdot \mathrm{Fluency}_J(h) + \varepsilon,$$

where $\mathrm{NN}*k$ is the top-$k$ retrieved neighbourhood, $\mathrm{Fluency}J$ is the judge's own likelihood of $h$, and $\varepsilon$ absorbs everything else. The intended part is $\alpha$; the mirage part is $\beta$. For $(h_G, h{\text{ref}})$ with $h_G \sim q_G$ and $h*{\text{ref}}$ human-written, $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Fluency}*J(h_G)] > \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Fluency}J(h{\text{ref}})]$ whenever $q_G \approx q_J$; the score gap then carries a systematic $\beta \cdot \Delta*{\mathrm{fluency}}$ term regardless of $\alpha$.

To make this tangible, a diagnostic sketch:

```python
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
phi = SentenceTransformer("all-mpnet-base-v2")
def retrieval_novelty(h, corpus_emb, k=10):
    e = phi.encode(h, normalize_embeddings=True)
    sims = corpus_emb @ e
    topk = np.sort(sims)[-k:]
    return 1.0 - float(topk.mean())
def fluency_proxy(h, judge_lm):
    # negative mean log-prob under the judge's LM; lower is more fluent to the judge
    return -judge_lm.mean_logprob(h)
def audit_scores(h_gen, h_ref, corpus_emb, judge_lm):
    return {
        "delta_retrieval": retrieval_novelty(h_gen, corpus_emb)
                         - retrieval_novelty(h_ref, corpus_emb),
        "delta_fluency":   fluency_proxy(h_gen, judge_lm)
                         - fluency_proxy(h_ref, judge_lm),
    }
Run this over a few dozen matched pairs from an existing benchmark (BioVerge or ResearchBench both expose the ingredients) and plot the deltas. If $\Delta_{\text{fluency}}$ is strongly negative and your judge's Likert score correlates more with $\Delta_{\text{fluency}}$ than with $\Delta_{\text{retrieval}}$, the mirage is on your bench. An afternoon; a first-order estimate of $\beta$ for the specific generator/judge pair you ship. My prior is that most self-scoring pipelines currently in the wild have $|\beta| > |\alpha|$ under standard prompts; a personal read from the RQ-Bench and Sakana data, not an established claim.
```

## What to do differently

Do not use a judge from the same model family as your generator. This is the single largest lever, and the RQ-Bench work is now enough evidence to treat it as default hygiene. If your generator is GPT-4o, your judge should be Claude Opus or Gemini or a bespoke fine-tune, and vice versa; a same-family judge is the ML equivalent of grading your own homework.

Report retrieval traces alongside novelty scores. Any deployed novelty score should ship with the list of retrieved neighbours it saw and the coverage statistics of that retrieval (how many hits, at what corpus size, over what time window). Reviewers can then check *whether the score was even in a position to detect prior work*. A high novelty score with three retrieved neighbours out of a corpus of ten million is not evidence.

Adopt temporal evaluation for hypothesis generation. BioDisco's protocol — train on literature up to time $T$, evaluate against discoveries first published in $[T, T + \Delta t]$ — is the cleanest available answer to contamination and self-preference at once. It is expensive to build but it is the only setup that measures the thing you want: predictive discovery, not paraphrase of the training set.

Require independent-team validation before shipping a claim. Google Co-Scientist's headline results are worth citing precisely because Imperial and Stanford confirmed them outside the loop. Any hypothesis-generation paper whose success metric is "our internal scorer preferred our system's outputs" should be read as a paper about the scorer, not the science.

## Limits and open questions

Everything above assumes novelty is a coherent target. It is not obviously one. A hypothesis can be novel and false; novel and untestable; novel and merely a synonym substitution over a known claim. BioDisco and RQ-Bench are beginning to unbundle novelty into *unlike prior work*, *unlike near-term extrapolations of prior work*, and *not derivable by trivial recombination*, but there is no consensus operationalization yet, and no reason to expect one across disciplines: what counts as novel in cheminformatics (a new scaffold, a new reaction class) has little structural in common with what counts as novel in social psychology (a new construct, a new moderator).

Truthfulness is less well-measured. Xiong et al.'s argument — evaluations reward plausible-reading hypotheses without checking whether they are grounded — is real, but their retrieve-and-verify remedy inherits the retrieval-scope-collapse problem. A hypothesis about a well-studied region is easy to verify and easy to mark unnovel; one about a sparsely-studied region is hard to verify and easy to mark novel. The wrong incentive gradient, unneutralized by any current benchmark.

The human-expert gold standard is not gold, either. RQ-Bench uses domain experts, and those experts disagree with each other at rates comparable to the noise in the ICML reviewer-agreement literature. Zhu et al. are careful to note that their expert scores are a distribution, not a label. Ranking systems by "expert-alignment" ranks them by alignment with a particular expert cohort; cross-cohort generalization is untested. Treat any single leaderboard number here as provisional.

What is not provisional: an internal LLM judge, applied to LLM-generated hypotheses, is a biased instrument. The bias is measurable, its mechanism is at least partly understood, and the correction — cross-family judges, retrieval traces, temporal evaluation, external validation — is not out of reach. State of the art, unstable enough to watch closely over the next year.

Trust the references; treat the numerical claims as secondary-source citations pending your own read.*

- Zhu et al., *On the Limits of LLM-as-Judge for Scientific Novelty Assessment*, [arxiv.org/abs/2606.12071](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12071). The primary source for the novelty-mirage claim and RQ-Bench.
- Xiong et al., *Toward Reliable Scientific Hypothesis Generation: Evaluating Truthfulness and Hallucination in Large Language Models*, IJCAI 2025, [arxiv.org/abs/2505.14599](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14599). The truthfulness-is-underevaluated argument.
- Ke et al., *BioDisco: Multi-agent hypothesis generation with dual-mode evidence, iterative feedback and temporal evaluation*, [arxiv.org/abs/2508.01285](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.01285). The temporal-evaluation protocol worth copying.
- Sun et al., *BioVerge: A Comprehensive Benchmark and Study of Self-Evaluating Agents for Biomedical Hypothesis Generation*, [arxiv.org/abs/2511.08866](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08866). The self-evaluation-helps counter-datapoint, honestly reported.
- Liu et al., *ResearchBench: Benchmarking LLMs in Scientific Discovery via Inspiration-Based Task Decomposition*, [arxiv.org/abs/2503.21248](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21248). The retrieval-vs-composition decomposition, the source of the $45.7%$ number for GPT-4o inspiration retrieval.
- Qi et al., *Large Language Models as Biomedical Hypothesis Generators: A Comprehensive Evaluation*, COLM 2024, [arxiv.org/abs/2407.08940](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08940). The publication-date partitioning trick for contamination-aware evaluation.
- Gottweis et al., *Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist*, *Nature* 2026, [nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10644-y](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10644-y). Google's multi-agent system and the antimicrobial-resistance and liver-fibrosis validations.
- Lu et al., *The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery*, Sakana AI, [sakana.ai/ai-scientist-nature/](https://sakana.ai/ai-scientist-nature/). The original AI Scientist paper, and the source of the 69% reviewer-accuracy figure.
- IEEE Spectrum, *The AI Scientist: A Tool from Sakana AI Stirs Up Controversy*, [spectrum.ieee.org/ai-for-science-2](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-for-science-2). The critical write-up that surfaced the micro-batching-for-SGD false-novelty example.
